newsitem.title: FRANCE: Eurotunnel holders talk of AGM debt plan block.
newsitem.headline: Eurotunnel holders talk of AGM debt plan block.

text.p: French shareholder associations fighting for better debt restructuring terms at Anglo-French Channel Tunnel operator Eurotunnel say they could have enough votes for a blocking minority at the annual meeting on July 10.

As the stakes rise between creditor banks and shareholders ahead of the July 10 general meeting, the radical ADACTE group and more moderate Eurotunnel Shareholders' Association said on Monday they could have enough votes to control the outcome.

They would need one third of the votes represented at the annual general meeting, said ADACTE deputy chairman Jean Salwa, whose group opposes the restructuring plan on the grounds that shareholders would lose out to creditor banks.
He said it was hard to tell for the moment how many votes his group would represent but that it was "two or three times" the roughly 10 million it represented at last year's meeting.

Christian Cambier, chairman of the Eurotunnel Shareholders' Association, said his group represented 25-30 million votes but had yet to take a final position and would decide whether to vote for or against the debt restructuring plan on July 2.

"We would have a blocking minority," Cambier said. Total shares come to some 920 million, of which there must be 25 percent represented at the meeting, and two thirds of the votes represented are necessary to back the restructuring.

Both groups said that an extraordinary shareholders meeting on Tuesday June 24 would not have enough votes present to make up the necessary quorum. The critical meeting was the ordinary shareholder's meeting on July 10.
Salva said small shareholder groups would need just over one-third of the votes represented to reject the restructuring plan.
"If we have 34 percent we can reject it," he said.
Another shareholder force is led by French lawyer Sophie L'Helias, who represents some institutionel investors.

She has set tough conditions on backing the plan, including that creditor banks abandon 25 percent of their loans and the possibility of a "right of substitution" wich would ultimately allow banks take over Eurotunnel.
